sections.h2: Who records deeds in Navajo County, Arizona?
sections.html:
The Navajo County Recorder records deeds and other real estate documents for the county. The office phone is 928-524-4194, and the counter is open Monday through Friday, 8:00 a.m. to 5:00 p.m.

Navajo County spans 9,960 square miles across northern Arizona, and the county seat is Holbrook. Many sellers live an hour or more from Holbrook, so the Recorder has set up two remote recording kiosks in other towns. The Recorder's web page also lists other county numbers worth keeping handy.

  • Snowflake Justice Court kiosk: 145 South Main Street, Suite D, in the main lobby, open Monday through Friday 8:00 a.m. to 4:30 p.m.
  • Navajo County Health Department kiosk, Show Low: 600 N. 9th Place, main lobby, open Monday through Thursday 8:00 a.m. to 4:30 p.m.
  • Assessor: 928-524-4086 for property assessment questions.
  • Treasurer: 928-524-4172 for tax bill questions.
  • Clerk of the Superior Court: 928-524-4188 for marriage and divorce records.

sections.h2: What are the recording fees in Navajo County?
sections.html:
Navajo County charges a $30 flat fee for all instruments. The fee applies whether the document comes back by mail or is recorded electronically, and the county's schedule notes that the Affidavit of Property Value form is included in the price of recording a deed.

Copies and certifications are priced per page and per document. The fee schedule cites A.R.S. 11-475 for the amounts and A.R.S. 11-480 for the rules a document must meet.

ItemNavajo County fee
All instruments$30
Government and state agencies$15
Copies of records, per page$1
Certified copy, per document$3
Survey or plat, first sheet / each additional$24 / $20
Copy of a map, 18 x 24 / 24 x 36 inches$5 / $7

Source: Navajo County Document Fee Schedule.

sections.h2: What must a deed look like before Navajo County will record it?
sections.html:
Navajo County's schedule spells out the layout rules from A.R.S. 11-480, and a deed that misses them can be turned away at the counter.

  • Print no smaller than ten point type.
  • Pages no wider than 8.5 inches and no longer than 14 inches.
  • At least a half-inch margin across the bottom of each page.
  • On the first page, a top margin of at least two inches of vertical space, left to right, kept clear for the recording stamp and return address.

If you drafted the deed yourself, check the first page against those numbers before you drive to Holbrook or a kiosk. The Recorder's page also advises that each document carry a title or caption that briefly states what it is.

sections.h2: Is there a transfer tax when you sell a house in Navajo County?
sections.html:
The county's fee schedule shows no charge based on the sale price. Arizona's Constitution, Article 9, Section 24, prohibits any new tax, fee or stamp requirement on the sale or conveyance of real property, with an exception for charges that already existed on December 31, 2007.

Instead of a tax, the state requires an affidavit. A.R.S. 11-1133 says every deed that transfers title must carry an Affidavit of Property Value signed by both sides, and the recorder must refuse the deed if the affidavit is incomplete and no exemption is noted. The affidavit asks for the total price, the down payment, the type of financing, the parcel number and whether the buyer will live in the house or rent it.

Gifts between close relatives, court-ordered conveyances and trustee's deeds are among the exemptions listed in A.R.S. 11-1134, and the deed must name the exemption it relies on.

sections.h2: What happens to the tax roll once a Navajo County deed is recorded?
sections.html:
The Treasurer's FAQ explains that ownership records update each time a deed is recorded with the Recorder. After that, the Navajo County Assessor changes the owner on the tax roll, and the change appears on the Treasurer's Property Information page the day after the Assessor enters it.

The Treasurer does not split a tax bill between buyer and seller. Property taxes attach to the property, and the title company prorates them on the settlement statement, giving the buyer credit for the seller's share. Check that statement before closing.

A seller who still receives the bill after closing can forward it to the new owner or mark the envelope sold and return it to the Treasurer. A manufactured home that was never affixed to the land is different: the old and new owners must tell the Assessor themselves, at 928-524-4086, once the title has moved.

sections.h2: How big is Navajo County and who lives there?
sections.html:
Navajo County was split from Apache County on March 21, 1895. It covers 9,960 square miles, and 6,632.73 square miles of that is federally designated reservation land, including parts of the Navajo Nation, the Hopi Reservation and the Fort Apache Reservation. That is the third-most reservation acreage inside any county in the country.

The 2020 census counted 106,717 people, and the Census Bureau's 2025 estimate is 109,946. There were 56,180 housing units, of which 34.4% were vacant, and 70.9% of occupied homes were owner-occupied. Show Low is the largest city, Winslow and Holbrook are the other two cities, and the towns are Snowflake, Taylor, Pinetop-Lakeside and Kayenta.

Interstate 40 runs through the county with business loops at Joseph City, Holbrook and Winslow, and State Routes 77 and 377 meet just south of Holbrook at the county government center. For a parcel inside a reservation boundary, ask the Recorder and a title company how the deed has to be recorded before you plan a sale.

sections.h2: How do you find liens, titles and deed copies in Navajo County?
sections.html:
The Recorder's FAQ list covers title searches, liens, the selling price of a property, copies of a deed and removing a decedent's name from a deed. Call 928-524-4194 to get the answers for your own parcel.

Copies are $1 per page, and a certified copy adds $3 per document. For a deed that still carries a deceased owner's name, the Recorder is the office that records the paperwork, and an attorney or title company decides which paperwork the situation calls for. Ask for that advice first so the recording is done once.

If taxes are unpaid, the Treasurer's Parcel Information Search shows the balance by parcel number, owner name or address, and the Treasurer's phone is 928-524-4172. The Navajo County property tax guide covers the dates and the lien process.

faqs.q: How much does it cost to record a deed in Navajo County, AZ?
faqs.a: It costs $30 for all instruments, whether the document is returned by mail or recorded electronically. Government agency instruments are $15, copies are $1 per page and certified copies are $3 per document.

faqs.q: Can I record a deed without driving to Holbrook?
faqs.a: Yes. Navajo County has remote recording kiosks at the Snowflake Justice Court, 145 South Main Street, Suite D, and at the Navajo County Health Department, 600 N. 9th Place in Show Low. Snowflake runs Monday to Friday and Show Low runs Monday to Thursday, both from 8:00 a.m. to 4:30 p.m.

faqs.q: Does Navajo County charge a transfer tax on a home sale?
faqs.a: The county's fee schedule lists no tax tied to the sale price. Arizona's Constitution, Article 9, Section 24, bars new taxes or fees on conveying real property, except those in place on December 31, 2007. A completed Affidavit of Property Value goes with the deed.

faqs.q: What are the formatting rules for a deed in Navajo County?
faqs.a: Use type no smaller than ten point, keep pages within 8.5 by 14 inches, leave a half-inch bottom margin and keep a two-inch blank strip at the top of the first page for the recording information. These come from A.R.S. 11-480.

faqs.q: Who updates the owner name on the property tax roll after a sale?
faqs.a: The Navajo County Assessor does, after the deed is recorded with the Recorder. The change shows on the Treasurer's Property Information page the day after the Assessor enters it. Call the Assessor at 928-524-4086 about a manufactured home title transfer.
